articles.title_orig: 'Unsettling to American partners': Trump’s offer to sell arms to China is an admission he doesn’t take its security threats seriously, experts warn
articles.title_zh: 'Unsettling to American partners': Trump’s offer to sell arms to China is an admission he doesn’t take its security threats seriously, experts warn
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump offered to sell weapons to China during President Xi Jinping’s recent summit in Washington, a move foreign policy experts said makes a mockery of U.S. warnings about the looming Chinese military threat.
In an interview with Fox News Sunday, David Purdue, the U.S. ambassador to China, suggested U.S. weapons are open to a multitude of countries, China included.
“President Trump continues to say, ‘Hey, we sell arms to other people around the world,’” he said. “He actually asked President Xi, would he like to buy some at one point.”
The White House said the U.S. government has no plans to sell weapons to China. The State Department did not immediately respond to Fortune ’s request for comment.
The comment baffled foreign policy experts, who argued the suggestion of selling weapons to Beijing would contradict the slew of sanctions and trade restrictions the Trump administration has placed upon the country, as well as dismiss China’s role in supplying munitions and military intelligence to Iran. The remark also came after reports China had obtained sensitive parts for the F-35 fighter that could be used to neutralize U.S. stealth technology.
“You would not [want to] help China to modernize its military and turn against yourself,” Zhiqun Zhu, professor of political science and international relations at Bucknell University, told Fortune . “Especially with the intense competition between the two powers now. I mean, it doesn’t make sense.”
While Trump has characterized China as a strategic competitor, and referenced that when rejecting calls to slow down AI development, the president has also expressed affinity for dictators like Xi, Russia’s Vladimir Putin, and North Korea’s Kim Jong Un.
As a result, Trump has often appeared to prioritize his personal ties with the leaders of U.S. adversaries to the detriment of U.S. allies.
“If there was any ambiguity about whether President Trump views China as a security threat, this disclosure by @USAmbChina Perdue puts the question to rest,” Ryan Hass, director of the Brookings Institution’s China center and senior fellow in the Center for Asia Policy Studies, wrote in a social media post on Sunday. “Trump’s offer to sell weapons to China will be unsettling to American partners at the pointy edge of China’s spear.”
Further complicating Trump’s suggestion of an arms sale to China is America’s preexisting commitments to provide arms to Taiwan, an independent island that China has continued to claim. The White House is withholding a $14 billion arms package and violating the 1979 Taiwan Relations Act , which was passed after the U.S. established diplomatic relations with China and requires the U.S. to provide necessary weapons for Taiwan to defend itself.
In May, senators signed a bipartisan letter to complete the sale. Ahead of Xi’s arrival at the White House last week, a group of Republican leaders led by Kentucky Sen. Mitch McConnell presented another letter to the Department of State and Department of Defense reiterating the need to finish the transaction.
Trump previously called the pending arms sale to Taiwan a “very good negotiating chip” with China. To Zhu, Trump’s tactics reveal what he is willing to give up or defy in order to maintain good relations with China.
“He still considers the arms sales as a leverage, as a bargaining chip at least,” Zhu said. “If China offers something really effective, it’s not inconceivable that he may further delay or even just temporarily cancel further arms sales to Taiwan.”
The simultaneous withholding of arms to Taiwan while offering a deal with China is a quintessential example of Trump’s interest in wielding commercial transactions as his chief method of diplomacy. In this instance, Zhu explained, Trump has little interest in actually engaging with China as a diplomatic partner, but is more concerned with making a deal that would mint the U.S. more money.
“He really viewed this as part of the commercial diplomacy he’s conducting,” Zhu said. “He views all these things as transactional. This is obviously from the U.S. perspective a very important geopolitical, geo-economic issue. But from Trump’s perspective, this is transactional. This has almost nothing to do with China.”
Trump has previously facilitated commercial arrangements with China, carving out an exception to the U.S. ban on sales of Nvidia and AMD chips to China. Despite the heated AI race, he allowed the companies to sell certain chips under a revenue-sharing model in which the U.S. receives a cut of up to 25%.
Trump has a history of mixing commerce and diplomacy elsewhere. Last year, the Trump administration brokered a peace deal between Armenia and Azerbaijan that granted the U.S. exclusive rights to build a transit corridor, dubbed the “Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity” that would run between the two countries.
While presidents for decades have employed the strategy of “transactional diplomacy,” few have prioritized financial gain over long-term national security advantages . Zhu believes in this instance, those two objectives are diametrically opposed.
“If this is a strategic issue, obviously, he will not offer arms sales to China to help China modernize its military,” he said.

The 10-year U.S. Treasury note yield —the key benchmark for mortgage borrowing, auto loans and credit card debt — was up more than 5 basis points at 5.234%.
The longer-dated 30-year Treasury bond yield, which is more sensitive to geopolitical risks, was 5 basis points higher at 5.552%.
The 2-year Treasury note yield, which tends to react in line with short-term Federal Reserve interest rate decisions, moved up by more than 6 basis points to 4.926%.
One basis point is equal to 0.01%, and yields and prices move in opposite directions.
Bond yields elsewhere also moved higher as anxiety surrounding global government debt and sticky inflation continue to weigh on investors.

Mediators are working with Iran and the United States on trying to broker a deal to end the fighting and open the Strait of Hormuz , three regional officials and two U.S. officials told The Associated Press, but major hurdles remain between the sides.
The indirect talks come as the conflict, which is entering its eighth month, has caused global economic damage and badly battered Iran. Multiple efforts to allow safe shipping on one of the world’s most crucial waterways have failed.
The officials divulged that the behind-the-scenes efforts continue even after U.S. President Donald Trump initially said he spurned an Iranian proposal to reopen the strait in a week if the U.S. agreed to lift its blockade of Iranian ports, release frozen Iranian assets and waive sanctions on Iranian oil sales, among other conditions.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi — who stayed in New York after last week’s gathering of world leaders at the U.N. General Assembly — will meet with Qatari mediators Monday about the latest discussions, Iranian state media reported Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmail Baghaei as saying.
Despite Trump’s often bellicose rhetoric, he is open to pursuing a non-military resolution to the conflict if one can be achieved, a senior U.S. official said.
But the Trump administration will not reach a deal with Tehran until nuclear issues are addressed, another U.S. official said. Trump is willing to grant sanctions relief to Iran, along with the release of some frozen funds, for concrete progress on nuclear issues, and while Iran has indicated it is flexible on nuclear issues, the sides are far apart on timing and which side makes the first moves, the official said.
All the officials were not authorized to comment publicly and spoke on the condition of anonymity about the behind-the-scenes diplomatic negotiations.
The deal would first reopen the strait and lift the US blockade
Two of the regional officials speaking to the AP confirmed that mediators are working with both sides on a proposal that would include reopening the strait and lifting the U.S. blockade, and then removing sanctions.
According to the draft text being discussed, the strait would reopen in accordance with a separate deal that Iran has been discussing with Oman, on the other side of the strait, and it would include no tolls — something Tehran has pursued. That deal seeks to temporarily manage shipping traffic on what was seen as an international waterway before the war.
One regional official said the U.S. is seeking Iranian concessions on nuclear issues that include allowing inspectors to enter the country. Under the memorandum of understanding the two sides signed in June that collapsed within days, Iran’s nuclear program was meant to be discussed over a 60-day period.
The U.S. officials say the United States is skeptical about whether Iran can be persuaded to ultimately reach Trump’s conditions for a deal and would be serious about any promises it makes, especially after it broke the interim deal by firing on commercial ships in the Strait of Hormuz.
U.S. officials feel their position is getting stronger as Tehran feels the impact of sanctions.
Iran's latest proposal seeks faster action
While Iran’s latest proposal echoes the June deal, a key difference is speed.
Araghchi told a closed-door meeting on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly last week that Tehran had pitched the deal as benefiting Trump in the midterm elections. Araghchi later told journalists that “the seven-day timeline will start as soon as the United States accepts this plan.”
U.N. Secretary-General Antonio Guterres also planned to meet Araghchi on Monday in a bid to help mediators, U.N. spokesman Stephane Dujarric said.
Both the U.S. and Iran have been hurting economically — the U.S. from high oil prices as Iran attacks ships on the strait, and Tehran from the naval blockade and a growing number of U.S. sanctions that bottle up its oil sales. Brent crude, the international standard, is above $108.
For months, the two sides have been trying to outlast the other, while regional countries endure missile and drone attacks as Tehran claims to target U.S. military assets in the region.
Reflecting Iran's impatience, a rare statement on Monday attributed to the theocracy's Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei noted the “painful blows” that enemy forces have received near the strait. “Before long, the Arabian Sea, too, will be rid of them,” the statement added.
Tehran's latest proposal again sought to end the fighting on all fronts, including in Lebanon. But a new front has emerged in recent weeks as Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen are now perched on another crucial waterway, the Bab el-Mandeb Strait at the southern entrance to the Red Sea. That has further pressured global energy markets.
Iran argues that the Houthis have their own demands, and that their conflict with neighboring Saudi Arabia is separate from the U.S.-Iran war, but Iranian officials said they are willing to help in finding a settlement between the Houthis and the Saudis, one of the officials said.
Price and Lee reported from Washington. Associated Press writers Collin Binkley in Washington and AP Middle East editor Victoria Eastwood contributed to this report.

Five men arrested on suspicion of terror offences near RAF Fairford on Sunday are released on bail , says the head of UK counter terrorism policing
Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor says the investigation is not over, and police are considering numerous angles, including if proxies working on behalf of a foreign state could have been involved
The men - all UK nationals in their 20s who live in London - were arrested under the Explosives Act and on suspicion of preparing a terrorist act
Police say they are "very aware of the levels of speculation about the motivation behind this incident, and the geopolitical questions that are being raised". The Iranian embassy in the UK denies any involvement
US President Donald Trump expressed surprise that the suspects have been released on bail
Meanwhile, Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood says that the scene is safe and residents will soon be allowed to return home
Earlier, a farmer who called 999 when she saw "a large group of hooded and masked men" said she "foiled" their plans. People living nearby say security had been ramped up before the arrests
There is still quite a lot of concern about what those men were doing so close to the RAF base, which is used by the US military, writes our correspondent
Edited by Andrew Humphrey and Caitlin Doherty
Gabriela Pomeroy Live reporter
The five men who were arrested on Sunday on suspicion of explosive and
terrorism offences near the RAF Fairford military base have
been released on bail, UK counter-terrorism police said this afternoon.
The men - who are all British - remain under investigation, "as we explore multiple lines of inquiry , the head of counter-terrorism policing, Laurence Taylor, told reporters.
Police are exploring whether proxies or individuals working on behalf of a foreign state were involved, he said.
The release of the five men sits at odds with our being told this was a "major incident ," the BBC's Security Correspondent Frank Gardner writes.
A large cordon remains in place near the base, while 85 households who were evacuated on Sunday have now been told by Gloucestershire Police that they can return home.
Many questions remain unanswered about the incident, including how President Trump's comments on the matter relate to the developments.
The US president said on Sunday: "We had them under investigation. They were looking to do big
damage.â
After the five men were released on Monday, Trump weighed in again, saying he wouldn't have let them out on bail.
We are ending our live coverage now but you can read our news story here .
Christopher Mace Live page reporter
Earlier we brought you a picture appearing to show an open and unguarded gate and barrier at RAF Fairford , reportedly taken on Thursday 24 September.
We sent the image to the United States Air Force this afternoon and they have now issued a response:
"For
operational security reasons we will not discuss specific force protection
measures.
"The 501st Combat Support Wing remains vigilant and will take
appropriate actions to ensure the safety and security of our US service
members, civilians, contractors, and their families across the European
theater."
They added: "We constantly assess a variety of factors that determine what measures
we institute or modify to protect our installations, our people and their
families."
Bernd Debusmann Jr White House reporter
As we've reported, President Trump was briefly asked about the incident at RAF Fairford.
His answers, however, did not provide much clarity - other than to make clear he was surprised and perhaps somewhat dismayed the five men arrested on Sunday have been released on bail, and that he views the co-operation with UK authorities as "very good".
While Trump said that Iran "might" be linked to the incident, he declined to provide any further details on what makes him believe that.
Since the US began striking Iran in late February, the White House and Trump have repeatedly described Iran's government as one that has been linked to terrorist attacks on US targets, stretching back to the founding of the Islamic Republic and bombings and kidnappings that took place in Lebanon in early 1980s.
Notably, there seems to be a disconnect between what Trump is saying and what British authorities are saying regarding the incident, with Trump saying that "we know everything" about the suspects and police in the UK stating that this was not an intelligence-led operation.
Speaking in the Oval Office, Trump says he wouldn't have let the five men arrested near RAF Fairford out on bail.
"I'm surprised they released them, I wouldn't have," he says.
"We know everything about them, we would not have released them."
He adds that the UK has been "very good" and has worked with the US "very closely".
US President Trump is currently speaking in the Oval Office - currently talking about domestic US matters - but we'll bring you anything he mentions on the RAF Fairford incident.
The incident is relevant to the US, as its air force operates out of the UK base, where its supersonic B-1 bombers are located.
Defence Secretary Wes Streeting has praised the policing response as "exemplary" following the incident near RAF Fairford, and says the men released are "under stringent bail conditions".
Speaking from Liverpool, following a Cobra meeting chaired by Andy Burnham, Streeting says that ministers are "acutely aware" that the events have "caused considerable disruption to the local community and also wider public concern".
He adds: "The response of our policing, counter-terrorism policing, and security services has been exemplary."
Streeting says that decisions around bail are for the police, and tells the public that "those five individuals are under stringent bail conditions", adding that "we remain with a live investigation".
Announcing that evacuated residents are able to return to their homes, Gloucestershire Constabularyâs Temporary Chief Constable Maggie Blyth has thanked the community for its "continued support and assistance".
She says she knows the incidents of the last few days will have caused "anxiety and uncertainty", but adds the force is doing "everything we can to return your lives to normality".
Blyth reiterates that Counter Terrorism Policing are leading the investigation, and that there are many questions  Gloucestershire Police "simply cannot answer".
She says the last 48 hours have thrown "our usually quiet and peaceful communities under the spotlight of the international media".
Blyth adds: "There have been some reports in the media that have raised questions about our response, and I want to reassure people we have responded appropriately and quickly to all calls."
Residents who were evacuated from around 85 homes near RAF Fairford because of a suspected plot to attack the airbase are now able to return home, Gloucestershire Police have said.
But police say a cordon remains in place
 around the three suspicious vehicles which were spotted near the military base in the early hours of Sunday morning.
People who were evacuated in the early hours of Sunday morning were taken to a nearby leisure centre which was set up for emergency respite.
Those who could not stay with family or friends were put up on Sunday night in hotels across Swindon and Cirencester.

"I could easily have walked onto or driven onto the base," he says.

articles.title_orig: Trump finalizes rule to make cars less fuel efficient
articles.title_zh: Trump finalizes rule to make cars less fuel efficient
articles.content_orig:
Traffic moves along the 405 Freeway on Feb. 13 in Los Angeles. Apu Gomes/Getty Images hide caption
Sign up for the Planet Money newsletter. The world is confusing. Economics can help
The Trump administration announced Monday it's scaling back how fuel efficient American carmakers need to make their fleets.
The Corporate Average Fuel Economy (CAFE) standards set average fuel economy levels for carmakers. The revised rules, which were finalized Monday, will now require carmakers to make their new passenger car and truck fleets up to 1% more fuel efficient each year, aiming for an average of 34.9 miles to the gallon in model year 2031.
This is down from Biden-era rules, which required an annual 2% increase in fuel efficiency with a goal of most vehicles getting, on average, 50.4 miles to the gallon by 2031.
The rationale: affordability. Administration officials argue that fuel efficiency technology is expensive, and has helped to drive up the cost of vehicles. They estimate that scaling back the standards will shave about $1,300 off the sticker prices of new cars.
"This administration is delivering relief to families and reviving the beating heart of American manufacturing," said U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy in an online statement announcing the change.
President Trump weighed in over the weekend on Truth Social : "These new Standards will take the waste out of building cars in America. That means LOWER PRICES, saving families thousands on a new, beautiful, and safe car."
Climate advocates and auto industry observers say the rules change is another step in the Trump administration's efforts to roll back Biden-era climate policies — including cutting the federal tax credit for electric vehicle buyers , delaying federal dollars for a nationwide EV charging program , and striking down federal waivers that let California set its own strict pollution regulations.
In a statement emailed to NPR, Dan Becker, director of the Safe Climate Transport Campaign at the Center for Biological Diversity, wrote that rolling back the standards would increase gasoline usage and pollution, "costing consumers at the pump and at the doctor's office."
"Trump is tanking sensible mileage standards at the worst possible time for consumers, who're getting hit with sky-high prices at the pump," he continued.
According to AAA , the national average price for gasoline today is close to $4.50 a gallon, and for diesel, a gallon is hovering close to $6.50, just short of last week's record high.
Easing CAFE standards will hinder the industry's realignment toward more fuel-efficient and electric vehicles, said economist Sue Helper, who studies the auto industry at Case Western Reserve University. "It's very bad in the long term, because it slows progress," she said. "Then we make our auto companies less competitive. We give them less practice in making the cars that both Americans will want in the future and that the rest of the world will want." After all, American carmakers hope to continue selling their cars in foreign markets that may have stricter emissions standards. And a future presidential administration could change the rules again.
CAFE standards have been part of the auto industry for decades. In 1975, during that decade's great oil supply shock, Congress enacted rules that encouraged carmakers to make their fleets more fuel efficient in an effort to reduce Americans' dependency on the Middle East for oil.
Since then, the national conversation about fuel efficiency has changed; the U.S. is now the world's largest oil producer, and many regulatory changes have instead been driven by concerns about climate change. Since the early 2010s, the fuel efficiency requirements for passenger cars and light trucks have consistently risen .
In practice, the Biden-era standards meant carmakers needed to make electric vehicles to balance out their gas guzzlers — otherwise they were subject to a fine.
But the Trump administration dropped that penalty last July as part of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, effectively defanging the Biden-era CAFE standards. In December, the White House proposed scaling them back altogether. Soon after, the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) opened a period of public comment .
In its final rule announcing the change, NHTSA also said it's eliminating the ability of carmakers to trade credits amongst themselves for making electric vehicles — a part of the Biden-era CAFE Standards that Republicans often criticized. This rule allowed automakers to buy credits from EV manufacturers to offset making less fuel-efficient vehicles. This helped them meet their CAFE targets.
In announcing the new change, the administration said lowering the CAFE standards will make cars cheaper.
"Instead of allowing manufacturers to design and produce vehicles they believe their customers will want and need, while spreading real-world fuel economy improvements across their fleets, the system has increasingly led manufacturers to try to fit square vehicle pegs in round classification holes to force the adoption of technologies that do not meet the demands of American families," stated NHTSA in the final rule. "All of this adds inefficiency and cost — pushing even more consumers out of an already unaffordable new car market."
"It's true that the price of new cars has gone up quite a lot," says Helper at Case Western. But she contends that much of that is not because of fuel economy standards. Instead, she says, it's because vehicles have gotten larger, they've faced tariffs and supply chain issues in recent years, and they are often loaded with extras like infotainment systems.
A Consumer Reports analysis from 2023 found that between model years 2003 and 2021, vehicles got about 30% more fuel efficient, but attributed the rise in prices to an industrywide shift toward expensive SUVs, rather than from using more fuel-efficient technologies.
And when it comes to the monthly costs of a new car, there are external factors beyond a carmaker's control — like the cost of an auto loan , which is affected both by the Federal Reserve's benchmark lending rate and by an individual buyer's credit score.
"One of the cruxes of vehicle affordability right now is the average monthly payment getting jacked up, because interest rates are so high," says Ellen Hughes-Cromwick, who spent much of her career as Ford's chief global economist and now studies clean energy as a senior visiting fellow at the center-left Third Way think tank.
Plus, a cut in the sticker price might eventually be offset by spending on gas. If vehicles are less fuel efficient, that means drivers will need to fill up at the pump more often — which is especially salient in a year of high gas prices due to the war in Iran.
For now, American carmakers are stuck in a kind of jam.
On the one hand, Helper said, a rules change that makes it easier for them to sell trucks and SUVs is "good in the short-term, because they make a lot of profits making these giant vehicles," though they are not as popular outside of the U.S.
This new move "allows the U.S. more of a playground in this protected little Galapagos of an ecosystem where no one else is wanting to compete," Helper continued.
But the Alliance for Automotive Innovation, a trade group representing car and light-truck manufacturers that sell vehicles to the U.S. and that includes automakers such as Ford, General Motors and Stellantis, praised the move. "We're still reviewing the final rule, but NHTSA made the right call to better align fuel economy standards with the law and current market conditions," said John Bozzella, president and CEO of the alliance, in an emailed statement to NPR.
"The standards finalized under the previous administration effectively required a switchover to electric vehicles that was out of step with market realities and customer demand. Today's final rule is an appropriate course correction," he continued.

articles.title_orig: Bond yields push higher as investors digest global risks, higher-for-longer path for the Fed
articles.title_zh: Bond yields push higher as investors digest global risks, higher-for-longer path for the Fed
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Yields on the longer end of the curve rose further to multidecade highs on Monday as a bond sell-off deepened.
The 10-year Treasury yield ( ^TNX ), often referred to as the most critical number in global finance for its widespread use as a benchmark rate, advanced roughly 5 basis points to 5.25%, its highest level since 2007, when yields rose in the run-up to the Great Financial Crisis.
Further out on the curve, 30-year Treasury yields ( ^TYX ) advanced by 6 basis points to 5.57%, a level not touched since 2004. The short end was also under pressure, as the 2-year yield ( 2YY=F ) rose by roughly 8 basis points to 4.93%.
Read more: How soaring Treasury yields could hit your finances
Bets on further rate hikes by the Federal Reserve, an energy crisis kicked off by the war in Iran, ballooning US government debt and budget deficits, and a historic investment cycle driven by the AI build-out have all contributed to a sell-off that has spooked investors.
Of those concerns, the Federal Reserve is perhaps the biggest focus for investors. Earlier in September, the Fed issued a quarter-point rate hike, raising the US target lending rate for the first time in three years.
"We now have data broadly defined that says the economy has indeed strengthened," Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh said in a press conference following the meeting. "Underlying growth is higher. Inflation is the problem. Stable prices have been the problem for now more than five and a half years."
More notable than the hike itself, however, were projections indicating that a majority of voting Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) members expected at least another quarter-point hike, reinforcing a higher-for-longer outlook for rates. Four FOMC members saw the need for the Fed to hike rates by 50 basis points in 2026.
The FOMC's price stability mandate has pushed the Fed to raise rates, per Warsh's statement. The war in Iran has made that mandate more consequential as it pushes up energy prices around the globe, increasing strain on businesses and consumers.
Read more: How the Fed rate decision affects your bank accounts, loans, credit cards, and investments
The AI boom has added another source of upward pressure.
A surge in spending on data centers, chips, power generation, and other infrastructure has helped keep US investment and economic growth resilient, even as financing costs have climbed. That strength can push yields higher by reducing the case for lower interest rates, while the enormous capital requirements of the build-out are adding to "competition for capital," or the demand for financing across the economy.
Taken together, those forces have driven investors to demand substantially higher yields on US government debt as they digest stronger growth, stickier inflation, expectations for tighter Fed policy, and a swelling supply of Treasurys needed to finance federal deficits. The result has been a sharp repricing across the curve.
Rising yields aren't necessarily bearish for growth, Macquarie global strategists Thierry Wizman and Gareth Berry argue. Rising Treasury yields often represent economic growth — when investors expect stronger activity, firmer demand, and continued wage increases.
"The reason to worry about the recent rise in long-term yields, if there is any, is not because they will slow the economy," the strategists wrote. "That way of thinking inverts the truer causality: yields are high partly because the economy is strong and bond issuance is high. And the economy is strong mainly because of the AI-induced infrastructure investment cycle."
Problems arise, Wizman and Berry wrote to clients on Monday, when yields rise too quickly, as they largely have since the start of the Iran war in late February.
Rapidly rising yields can "fall disproportionately on one company, lender, or whole sector that had over-leveraged in the low-yield environment of 2021," the strategists wrote. Even if that outcome remains contained, concerns can still trigger volatility in the wider market.
Investors will be carefully watching this week's US PCE price-change report — the Fed's preferred measure of inflation — and Friday's September jobs report, both set to be key macro indicators for the FOMC's path forward.

articles.title_orig: Alito bows out of blockbuster Supreme Court climate case
articles.title_zh: Alito bows out of blockbuster Supreme Court climate case
articles.content_orig:
Supreme Court Justice Samuel Alito , in a surprising reversal, has recused himself from participating in a major climate-change case the Supreme Court is set to hear next week, which involves the oil companies Exxon Mobil and Suncor Energy .
Environmental groups had called on Alito, one of the court's six conservative justices, to not participate in the case because of his holdings of stock in oil and gas companies. Alito does not hold stock in Exxon Mobil or Suncor Energy, according to his most recent financial disclosure for 2025.
Alito previously refused to step off the case after the Supreme Court accepted it for consideration earlier this year. However, in 2023, he did not participate in the court's decision not to consider jurisdictional questions raised by the companies in the same case.
The case, known as Suncor Energy (USA) Inc. v. County Commissioners of Boulder County, is focused on the question of whether federal law precludes claims made under state law seeking damages for injuries allegedly caused by climate change to greenhouse gas emissions.
The case is set to be argued on Oct. 5.
"I am writing to inform the parties that Justice Alito has determined that he will not continue to participate  in this case," Scott Harris, the clerk of the Supreme Court, wrote lawyers for the parties in the case, on Monday.
Alito's sudden recusal sets up the possibility of a 4-4 split ruling on the Supreme Court in the case. A tie in a Supreme Court decision leaves in place the lower-court decision that was being appealed.
The case involves a lawsuit by the city of Boulder, Colorado, and its surrounding county, that seeks damages for alleged harms from the effects of global climate change. A trial court denied a motion to dismiss that was filed by Suncor and Exxon, and the Colorado state Supreme Court affirmed that ruling, allowing the suit to head to trial.
If the Supreme Court rules against the oil companies, the case would proceed toward trial.
In May, a Supreme Court spokeswoman told NBC News that Alito would not step aside from the case.
"Justice Alito does not have a financial interest in any party" involved in the case, the spokeswoman told NBC News at the time.
She added that the Supreme Court's legal counsel had advised Alito that "his recusal is not required," according to NBC.

articles.content_orig:
Raoni Barcelos was hospitalized after the UFC defeat
Raoni Barcelos is “doing great” despite the frightening scenes in his UFC Vegas 121 main event loss to Raul Rosas Jr. this past weekend at the Meta APEX.
The 39-year-old bantamweight was ahead in the scorecards going into the final round and blacked out and collapsed unconscious for apparent no reason with less than three minutes left in the fight.
The UFC and Barcelos’ team have yet to reveal what caused the incident, but the veteran fighter shared his first words in the comment section of a UFC Brasil post on social media.
“Hey everyone, I just want to let you all know that I’m doing great, and as soon as I can, I’ll send a video to all of you,” Barcelos wrote in Portuguese. “Thank you so much for everyone’s love, support, and prayers! I promised a great fight, and I delivered on that promise. Thank God, and thank you to everyone who fought alongside me, both inside and outside that cage.”
On Sunday, just hours after the fight, Barcelos’ head coach Davi Ramos released a statement to comfort fans, saying the athlete was “conscious” and under medical care in Las Vegas.
“Raoni is doing well,” Ramos said Sunday. “He has all his senses, he’s moving his leg, his arm, his hand, he’s conscious, he’s talking, everything is fine with him. He’s undergoing some tests, and pretty soon he’ll be here to talk to you guys.”
“I just wanted to let you know so you can all stay calm,” he continued. “Keep praying for him. He’s undergoing all the tests that are standard in a situation like this. He’ll have to rest because of what happened, but God willing, everything will be fine. He’ll be here with us soon and he’ll be talking to you guys. Thank you to everyone who’s been sending messages, positive energy, praying and keeping all of us in your prayers.”
Update : Ramos posted a video on social media from outside the hospital, standing next to other trainers, including Barcelos’ father Laerte Barcelos, where he ruled out a stroke and heart attack. There’s still no official work on what caused the issue.
“He did not have a stroke, it wasn’t a heart attack, nothing like that, but we still don’t have an explanation for what happened,” Ramos said. “We’re waiting for the results of the other tests. But he is doing well.”
Laerte joked that his son is desperate to be discharged from the hospital. According to his team, Raoni Barcelos is expected to post a video statement on social media soon.

Andrew Bailey is stepping down as one of the FBI 's two deputy directors after slightly more than a year in the role, stating on Monday that he plans to return home to Missouri to spend time with his family.
His tenure began in August 2025 when he was appointed co-deputy director alongside Dan Bongino during a period of high tensions between the FBI and Justice Department leadership regarding the handling of the release of the Jeffrey Epstein files.
Having two individuals share the deputy director position marked a significant departure from the bureau's long-standing tradition of appointing a single person to its No. 2 job.
A former attorney general from Missouri and ardent Republican supporter of President Donald Trump, Bailey stayed in his post following Bongino's departure.
He remained when veteran agent Christopher Raia was added as another deputy director in January to serve under Director Kash Patel.
Confirming his resignation from the FBI in a post on X on Monday, Bailey expressed gratitude to Trump, Attorney General Todd Blanche, and Patel for "the opportunity to serve in the FBI."
"With great pride in what we have accomplished, I am announcing that I am stepping down to return to my family in Missouri. I am confident Director Patel will continue to reform the FBI, combat violent crime, defend the homeland, ensure strong organizational accountability, and restore public trust in this institution of excellence," Bailey wrote.
In his own post, Patel praised him for his "dedicated service" and recognized his role in "instituting critical reforms."
Throughout his brief period as deputy director, Bailey largely maintained a low public profile.
However, he was present in January when agents executed a search warrant at the main election facility in Fulton County, Georgia, as part of an FBI election fraud investigation.

articles.title_orig: Best thing we can offer young people is a job, not benefits, says chancellor
articles.title_zh: Best thing we can offer young people is a job, not benefits, says chancellor
articles.content_orig:
The chancellor has warned against allowing Britain's benefits bill to balloon while not offering young people opportunities.
John Healey told Labour's annual conference in Liverpool that cutting welfare spending was "more than an economic must - it's a moral duty".
"The best thing we can offer a young person is not a benefit payment - it's a first job with training and a wage," he said.
He announced the expansion of a Local Apprenticeships Service for mayors in England, which he said would deliver thousands more apprenticeships for young people.
Healey's speech comes as he faces pressure to cut public spending or raise taxes ahead of next month's Budget to bring down government borrowing costs.
In an attempt to reassure the markets, he said all promises the government made would be "built on the rock of fiscal discipline" with him and Prime Minister Andy Burnham "united on meeting the fiscal rules".
Fiscal rules are the government's self-imposed constraints to manage decisions on spending and tax.
The Budget would "give families and businesses a bit of breathing space", the chancellor said.
And he admitted that "the money New Labour had in the '90s is simply not there now".
Healey blamed the Conservative Party's time in government for leaving Britain spending more on debt than on the Home Office, Ministry of Defence and Ministry of Justice combined.
Tory shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith said in response to the speech that "Labour MPs will never support cutting the out-of-control welfare bill" and "with Labour, it's always more taxes if you work and more benefits if you don't".
Healey praised young people as "digital natives, whip-smart, questioning, ambitious, brave" who could move from "generation jeopardy to generation hope".
But he pointed to the million young people not in education, employment or training - known as Neets - which he said created a necessity to make benefits a bridge into work, rather than a "trap".
"It is not progressive to allow a bigger and bigger benefits bill, and a system which offers an income but doesn't offer a future," he said.
Asked how quickly the bill might come down, when he appeared on the BBC's Newscast , Healey would not commit to the benefits bill falling, saying he "won't set a timeline" for the UK's benefits bill coming down by the time of the next election.
The Local Apprenticeships Service was initially planned as a pilot in a limited number of areas but would now be available to any English mayor who wants it, he said.
Through the scheme, which the Treasury says will roll out across England from March 2027, local teams plan to match young people with employers, including small businesses that have never taken on a trainee.
The department said an extra £100m was going into the scheme, "fully funded" by savings from the Department for Work and Pensions' crackdown on fraud.
Powers to implement the scheme will rest with mayors because "they know which firms are hiring, which colleges are delivering, which estates have been left behind," Healey said.
It comes as the final instalment of a major report by former minister Alan Milburn is expected to set out recommendations for tackling the one in eight people aged 16 to 24 in the UK who are Neets in the coming weeks.
Healey said these young people had been "signed off, written off" which the Labour government would address.
Helen Miller, director of the Institute for fiscal studies think tank, told the BBC that sticking to fiscal rules alone would not be enough to reduce debt because it is "basically a promise to get down debt tomorrow".
She suggested that reducing the benefits bill, including removing support from some people, could be one way of cutting the national debt sooner.
Elsewhere in his speech, Healey repeated his promises to re-industrialise the country and said Rolls Royce would invest £300m more into its British factories in Derby, Bristol, Glasgow and Rotherham.
He also said he was bringing back the Union Learning Fund in England, established in 1998 and abolished by the Tories, to help working people gain more skills in an age of artificial intelligence. It was initially unclear how this would be funded.
Healey did not set out a pathway for greater defence spending in his speech, another area of pressure for ministers.
And he declined to commit to the pensions triple lock being in Labour's next manifesto, when asked several times by BBC Radio 5 Live's Matt Chorley, after speculation it may be dropped to help fund a new social care system .

Apple debuted the all-new AirPods 5 this month, and they bring ANC to lower prices than ever before. If you’re shopping for AirPods, however, there are still several reasons you might want to opt for the more expensive AirPods Pro 3.
AirPods are one of Apple’s most personal products. The fit can vary dramatically between different people depending on the size of their ears. AirPods 5 offer an open-ear design, so they rest on the inside of your ear. AirPods Pro, meanwhile, offer a more traditional in-ear design with ear tips.
Personally, I find AirPods Pro to be more comfortable than AirPods 5. They’re also more secure for me, so I’m less worried they’ll fall out of my ears.
One of the key differentiators between AirPods Pro 3 and AirPods 5 is that AirPods Pro 3 offer built-in heart rate monitoring capabilities. During a workout, AirPods Pro can measure your heart rate to provide additional fitness metrics.
If you wear an Apple Watch, AirPods Pro 3 work along with your Apple Watch to ensure you get the most accurate data possible. Apple’s algorithms monitor the data from AirPods Pro and Apple Watch, and factor in the type of workout you’re doing, to use the most consistent data possible. For example, if you’re lifting weights and the Apple Watch ends up at an awkward angle on your wrist, AirPods Pro 3 will step in to provide more accurate data.
Furthermore, in iOS 27, Apple brought GymKit to the iPhone, so you can use iPhone and AirPods to get an Apple Watch-style experience … but without wearing a watch. Learn more about this change in Zac’s full coverage .
AirPods Pro 3 offer a range of hearing health features that aren’t available on AirPods 5. This includes:
With the Hearing Test feature, you can take a 5-minute test to identify if you have hearing loss. Apple’s Hearing Aid feature, meanwhile, is a clinical-grade hearing aid that uses the results of your test to craft a sound profile for your needs. Finally, Hearing Protection, can help prevent exposure to loud environmental noise.
There are other reasons to choose AirPods Pro over AirPods 5, including longer battery life, even better ANC, and a more capable charging case. The difference in ANC, in particular, is notable: Apple says AirPods Pro 3 offer 3x more Active Noise Cancellation than AirPods 5.

As all-in-one AI agents like Meta’s Muse and Instinct take off, Google announced it’s shutting down the Gemini feature known as “ Gems ,” which had allowed users to build custom AI assistants for specific tasks. However, the work users invested in creating the Gems won’t be destroyed. Gems will be automatically migrated to “skills” that can be used across different AI tasks.
Details about the change are being shared in the Gemini app, where a message warns users that Gems will become skills starting on November 17, 2026. The company said it will migrate the Gems to the new format, so users won’t have to do anything to make the transition. The Gems themselves will remain usable until then.
Launched in 2024, Gems were meant to help users teach their AI to perform certain tasks without having to repeat the instructions. For instance, some of Google’s premade Gems had included a learning coach, a brainstorming assistant, a career guide, a coding partner, and an editor. Users could also make Gems for their own needs, like a running coach, nutritionist, or vacation planner. These custom assistants could also be shared with others, which Google had hoped would help make its Gemini AI app more popular.
The news of Gems’ shutdown is another example of why Google shouldn’t be so quick to give every new AI feature its own brand name, icon, and prominent placement in its app’s navigation — especially if it’s going to shuffle things around over time, merging one feature into another. (To be clear, this has been a failing point of Google’s strategy long before the AI era. At one point, for instance, the company was operating multiple different messaging and communication apps at the same time.)
Yet, even as skills, the former Gems still aren’t as consumer-friendly as just typing in text to a chatbot like Meta’s Muse. Instead, Google notes you’ll have to enter a forward slash “/” in a task thread to select the skill you want to use — a user interface that engineers, not regular folks, tend to prefer.
Gems’ wind-down was first reported over the weekend by 9to5Google .

The designer statistic is the NFLâs silent assassin. Seemingly every outlier performance, both good and bad, is accompanied by a computer-generated information nugget that lets us know that teams in a similar position are a combined 987â1 when leading by three touchdowns in late September, when the temperature crests 72Â°, and the crescent moon hangs over the meadow. The songbirds sing of loversâ past, with your idiot team being the only one that has lost in that situation. I never know what to do when I see those, and also is anyone else with a supercomputer fact-checking these? Iâm not saying the computer is wrong, but it would be pretty easy for me to drop a stat like this into the ether, and everyone else would be like, Yeah, that sounds right. Â
Anyway, this one is infinitely more verifiable but similarly useless. I donât know what to do with the information that Klint Kubiak is the first head coach to begin the season 3â0 after his team had the No. 1 pick the previous season since Vince Lombardi. Similarly, I donât know what to do with the information that the previous two Raiders coaches to start their first season 3â0 were John Madden, who went to the AFC title game in that 1969 season, and Bill Callahan, when the Raiders made it to the Super Bowl in 2002.Â
Which is why I think a post on assessing the âsurpriseâ teams through three weeks of the 2026 season is due. We can snack on AI-generated tidbits all we want about Kubiak and the Raiders, but we should dive into the circumstances by which this came to be a surprise and, through that exploration, decide whether it matters all that much. Along with the Raiders, weâll get into a few other teams in similar circumstances, though they wonât all be 3â0.
Iâm going to rate each team by the highly scientific ârealnessâ rating. These teams are either âextremely real,â âpretty darn real,â âa perfectly normal amount of real,â ânot all that real,â orâgaspâânot real at all.â Indeed, people who read this article all the way to the end boast a 68.7% chance of experiencing a moment of immense personal joy.Â
Realness: Pretty darn realÂ
Why: Hereâs a wild statistic about the Raiders that I think matters. The Raidersâ defense has forced eight fumbles and recovered one. That kind of luck differential doesnât seem to matter for a team that is maximizing its drives better than almost any other team in the NFL. Through three weeks, the Raiders have punted only 12 times, with a handful of those coming in garbage time. The Raiders have also scored on two of their three scripted drives at the beginning of the game. Las Vegas is one of the 10 teams most likely to end its drive in a touchdown so far this year, and while weâre still operating with an incredibly small sample size and one of the Raidersâ wins was against the Dolphins, a team that overwhelmingly has the highest odds to attain the No. 1 pick in 2027, what we saw on Sunday against a more formidable Saints team looks to be the Raiders weâll be getting for a majority of the year.Â
In Sundayâs win, the Raiders became a 12-personnel team (one running back, two tight ends). That isnât all that surprising given that Brock Bowers returned and, if two of your five best offensive players are tight ends, youâll want them on the field together. But the Raiders won a game (Week 1) in which they were a majority 21-personnel team (a two-back, typically fullback-oriented offense) and a Week 2 game in which they were primarily an 11-personnel team (one running back, one tight end and three wideouts). Now that Bowers is on the field, and he played primarily as a wide receiver against the Saints, it gives the Raiders a kind of peak-49ers-like versatility that makes the team very difficult to prepare for. At the very least, we now know the Raiders arenât going to be run over. Having come into the week with the leagueâs best pass-block win rate, Kirk Cousins will remain relatively comfortable in the pocket and, all of a sudden, projecting six wins out of the teamâs remaining schedule (without any real upsets) doesnât seem ridiculous whatsoever. The Raiders still have games with the Titans, Cardinals, Jets, Browns and the limping Patriots, and, oh by the way, the calling card of a true Kubiak tree offenseâthe ground gameâhasnât even found its footing yet.Â
Defensively, the Raiders remind me of the 2025 Bearsâ offense in that theyâre enjoying health and peak performance from a handful of newly imported free agents. The Raidersâ remake of their linebacking corps has been nothing short of transformative.Â
Realness: A perfectly normal amount of real
Why: The Steelers are 2â1, and while we cannot in the same breath celebrate the Raidersâ win over the Dolphins and completely discount a narrow Steelers victory over the Falcons in the opener, we can point out two very different circumstances in those games. Pittsburgh, for one, needed a miraculous defensive play to edge a really bad Cooper Rushâled Falcons team. The Steelers deserve immense credit for dressing down a Bengals defense that came into this game in the top five in sacks, touchdowns allowed, passing touchdowns allowed, yards per game allowed and turnovers created. But we saw what is still possibleâand the defining upsideâof the Aaron RodgersâMike McCarthyâera Steelers: creating embarrassing coverage busts against the Bengals. The Cincinnati secondary was on ice skates, though Iâm almost certain Rodgers will never have pocket time like this again. Rodgers averaged a season-high 3.19 snap-to-throw time Sunday, and Jaylen Warren gouged the Bengals for 7.5 yards per carry. That allowed Rodgers to be more effective in play-action, which the Steelers used on more than 20% of his dropbacks for a 1.14 EPA per play. To McCarthyâs credit specifically, some of the concepts heâs been playing withâlike a Rams-ian, Seahawks-ian Ben Skowronek insert concept that created an open touchdownâshows that the old ball coach can still dig into his bag and dial up some impressive shots.Â
DK Metcalf appearing to get over whatever was bothering him over the first two weeks of the seasonâPittsburgh had lost the most EPA per play to drops in the NFL to that pointâis also a major upgrade.Â
The debut of Max Iheanachor was encouraging, with the rookie offensive tackle allowing the lowest pressure percentage of any of Pittsburghâs offensive linemen on Sunday. If Iheanachor turns into a great drop-back anchor tackle, I may increase my optimism levels because giving the most arm-talented quarterback of his generation light-years of time in the pocket is a sound strategy if itâs replicable.Â Â
Iâm a little more muted in my praise at the moment because I want to see what a very old Steelers team looks like on short rest against a division rival in a suddenly-hostile environment (weâll get to that Week 4 game against the Browns in a moment) and then a matchup against a Colts team that could test Pittsburghâs so-far mediocre run defense, which is allowing above a 40% success rate to opponents this season.Â
That should give us a better sense of whether the perceived strengths of this teamâagain, an offensive line that could be very, very good, and a pass rush that, so far, has a success rate about as high as the vaunted Vikingsâcan hold up over a long period of time.Â
Realness: Not all that real (yet)

Mason Graham showed as much on Sunday in a win over the Panthers in which he was virtually unblockable. He registered seven pressures and two sacks, equally as masterful in the stunt game as he was against double teams. Alphabet CEO Sundar Pichai will also be at the lunch, the company confirmed Monday, as well as Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, according to MS Now. OpenAI President Greg Brockman will be in attendance as well, Reuters reported, citing a person familiar with the matter.
Trump, Vice President JD Vance and other administration officials are hosting an all-day event on Tuesday to announce a new website for federal information and resources, according to a White House official. That event will have panel discussions on artificial intelligence , energy, space and other topics.
Anthropic co-founder and Chief Compute Officer Tom Brown will also be in attendance at the event, according to a person familiar with the plans, who spoke on condition of anonymity because the details are not public.
Last week, multiple big tech executives attended the state dinner for the visit of Chinese President Xi Jinping, including Apple's Tim Cook, SpaceX's Elon Musk and Advanced Micro Devices CEO Lisa Su.
Amodei, who was notably absent from Thursday's China state dinner, had a private dinner with the president on Sunday. It was the first one-on-one meeting between the two leaders, according to a person familiar with the visit, who asked not to be named in order to discuss a confidential matter.
Tuesday's meeting could serve as another opportunity for tech leaders, particularly Amodei, to ease tensions with the White House as the debate over AI safety has spread and leaders have taken sides on potential regulation. A former Anthropic researcher triggered the outcry after he accused AI frontier labs of "gambling with our lives."
Industry leaders like OpenAI chief Sam Altman and Musk have agreed with calls for an industry-wide slowdown, after Amodei penned an essay calling for companies to "pace the frontier" with advanced AI. articles.title_zh: Leo’s visit across France offers a more personal glimpse of the pope
articles.content_orig:
France may have a highly secularized culture, but it has given Pope Leo XIV a superstar welcome.
In Paris, around 800,000 lined the Champs-Élysées avenue, some waving Vatican or French flags while others climbed trees or stood on each other’s shoulders to get a glimpse of the popemobile. In Lourdes, a holy site in southern France, around 150,000 attended an open-air papal Mass, according to Vatican estimates which dwarf the numbers of faithful who turned out for the last papal visit in 2008.
During the four-day visit, Leo appeared comfortable and relaxed, delivering most of his speeches and reflections in French, as the Chicago-born pontiff sought to tackle several themes during the trip.
A strong focus of Leo’s has been on trying to revitalize faith in a traditional European Catholic heartland as well as on addressing the clerical sexual abuse scandal and big political topics such as artificial intelligence. He’s also offered some more personal, unscripted remarks, helping to shape a clearer picture of himself.
While his predecessor never made official visits to the major Catholic European countries of France and Spain, Pope Leo has traveled to both within the first year and a half since his election.
France is sometimes described as the “eldest daughter of the church” because of its deep Catholic roots, but it’s also faced a long-term trend of declining church attendance with estimates of just 5-8% of the population heading to the pews each week.
French bishops have more recently reported some good news though: a surprising rise in new church entrants after around 8,200 adolescents and 13,200 adults were baptized in 2026. That’s a 20% increase on the year prior, with the church also saying 42% of the adults seeking baptism are aged 18-25, a reflection of a trend showing Gen Z’s openness to religious faith .
It’s something Pope Leo will have noted at the Stade de France when 80,000 young people packed the venue for a jubilant – and loud – prayer vigil. It was similar to when the pontiff visited Spain in June.
“There is a quest for meaning. People need and are in search of meaning and answers to the big existential question,” Rev. Benoît Pouzin, a priest in southwest France involved in youth ministry, told CNN.
France has a strict separation between church and state, so each papal visit needs to be carefully navigated. But in a surprising twist, Leo’s Mass in Paris was celebrated on the Place de la Concorde, a site deeply linked to the secular Republic as it’s where the last king of France, Louis XVI and Marie-Antoinette were guillotined. The separation of the church started with the fall of the monarchy during the French Revolution.
In another unusual move later in the trip, President Emmanuel Macron also attended a papal Mass in Metz, a city in the northeast, despite criticism in 2023 for doing the same during Pope Francis’ visit.
Many among the crowds also pointed to Leo’s role as the other major US leader on the world stage. It’s hard not to see him as a counterweight to President Donald Trump. In contrast to the Trump administration, the pope has called for stronger guardrails around the development of artificial intelligence, warning against a “paradise of machines” while in Paris.
Pope Leo said he is taking the warnings about Artificial Intelligence’s threat to humanity seriously, and said it is irresponsible for people to sit back and dismiss the risks of AI.
Trump has dismissed the warnings about AI as a “hoax” which he made during a surprise phone call with Jensen Huang, the CEO of chipmaker Nvidia, at a summit in Los Angeles.
“I don’t think that that is fake news – as some have said – to try and pause,” Leo XIV said on board the papal plane from Metz to Rome.
Leo, who has expressed a keen interest in artificial intelligence since the start of his papacy, said that he found it “interesting” that Huang had unveiled a new tool to prevent AI agents from operating out of human control.
“He’s the same one, however, that says there should be no limits placed and no government regulation,” the Pope said.
The pope devoted his first major theological document to AI earlier this year, warning about the use of AI in warfare and calling for stronger ethical foundation to the development of the technology.
The pope explained that the Vatican had established its own AI commission to understand how to use it, along with the risks and benefits, and that “we need to continue to invite political leaders, the leaders of AI” so they can “look at what is happening already and what could be down the road.”
He explained: “We are trying to continue to promote dialog, study, investigation, to find ways to make sure that AI does not get to a point where it could destroy humanity.”
“If someone were to ask me, am I in panic mode? No, I’m not, I sleep at night” the pope said, but added: “I do think that the concerns raised by many of the experts, specialists in AI, should be taken seriously.”
“To simply say, oh, it’s not going to happen and close our eyes to it, I think, is probably not the most responsible way to go about that,” Leo said.
The pope, who spoke out against the US war in Iran, also wants a more united Europe, a stronger European Union and stronger international cooperation. “Today, relations between individuals and states are becoming increasingly uncivilized,” the pope said in Metz on Monday. “The value of keeping one’s word is dismissed; instead, people boast of lies and deceit.”
The pope’s speech also praised one of the founders of the European Union, Robert Schuman, for whom there is an ongoing formal cause to make a saint.
Pope Leo XIV has warned against the use of Christianity by far-right political groups, while calling on the church to be active in seeking to prevent extremism. Speaking on board the papal plane, he said that “the combination of these far-right points of view with a certain kind of religion” cannot be considered an “authentic expression of Christianity.”
The pope’s comments came in response to a question about the rise of extremist parties in Germany as he flew back from making a major speech on European Unity at the French-German border.
“We go back to the values of the Gospel [Christian teaching], which are not about hatred and division, but they’re about understanding and compassion,” the pope said.
The American pontiff also responded to Trump’s White House media ban, which includes CNN and other outlets. In answer to a question from CNN, he said he was “very happy that, here, you are all welcome and good coverage, I think, is very important and that we have it all the way around, for everyone.” The response was classic Leo: signaling his support for the press but not wishing to create an unnecessary dispute with the president.
The American pope’s in-flight interactions with journalists were rare, unscripted moments, with his answers often revealing more about his personality. On the flight from Rome to Paris, the pope was asked if he had anything to do with a miraculous recent Chicago White Sox victory, his beloved baseball team. “No comment,” he said before adding with a smile, “Great things happen in Chicago.”
He also recalled childhood memories of watching Fulton Sheen, the American archbishop and broadcaster who was recently declared “blessed,” one step ahead of sainthood, and revealed he’d been practicing his French but was no longer using the Duolingo language app. “It’s fake news!” he said about recent reports. Leo has in the past been spotted using Duolingo to learn German.
Leo isn’t simply vocal about challenges of his homeland. He also voiced concern over assisted dying with France recently approving legislation granting the right to the incurably ill, which is strongly opposed by the Catholic Church. Leo spoke on the subject several times during his visit – most clearly in the “miracle shrine” town of Lourdes, known for drawing many sick and terminally ill pilgrims to its shrine.
